cards.explanation: The king says it could only be sadness of the heart. He asks, "Why is your face sad, though you are not ill? This could only be sadness of the heart." (Nehemiah 2:2) Nehemiah had just handed King Artaxerxes the wine, and he had never been sad in the king's presence. (Nehemiah 2:1) A king can tell when something's off, friends.

The answer is False. Nehemiah says, "I was overwhelmed with fear" when the king asks about his face. (Nehemiah 2:2) He wasn't calm and he wasn't cool. I've been there, friends, my knees knocking like a loose cookie sheet. He answers anyway, and that takes real courage.

Nehemiah says the city lies in ruins and its gates are burned, and he says it plainly: "Why should I not be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins, and its gates have been destroyed by fire?" (Nehemiah 2:3) Notice he doesn't say "Jerusalem." He calls it the city where his fathers are buried. I think that tells you how close to home it hits.

Before he answers, Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven. The king asks, "What is your request?" and the very next line says, "So I prayed to the God of heaven" (Nehemiah 2:4) The king has just asked his question, and Nehemiah still prays before he answers. I'd have blurted something out and then needed a nap.
The word is rebuild. Nehemiah asks the king to send him to Judah "…so that I may rebuild it." (Nehemiah 2:5) He isn't asking for a vacation, friends. He wants to put the city back together.

The answer is True. The king, with the queen seated beside him, asks, "How long will your journey take, and when will you return?" (Nehemiah 2:6) Right after that, the text says, "So it pleased the king to send me…" (Nehemiah 2:6) I'd call that a good sign, friends.

The letters are so the governors will grant him safe passage. Nehemiah asks for letters "…so that they will grant me safe passage until I reach Judah." (Nehemiah 2:7) He's thinking ahead, friends. A letter from the king is like having the best pass in the whole kingdom.

The word is forest. Nehemiah asks for "…a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king’s forest…" (Nehemiah 2:8) Timber is what he's after. When I need chocolate chips I reach for the jar, but this man writes a letter to the keeper of a whole forest!

Nehemiah says it happened because the gracious hand of his God was on him. His words are: "…because the gracious hand of my God was upon me, the king granted my requests." (Nehemiah 2:8) He doesn't pat himself on the back. He gives the credit to God, and I admire that. Nice lesson for all of us, friends.

The answer is False. The text says, "The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me." (Nehemiah 2:9) So Nehemiah had soldiers riding along with him. That's a lot more company than I had in my old drawer, friends.

The two words are disturbed and well-being. Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official "…were deeply disturbed…" (Nehemiah 2:10) Sanballat and Tobiah are brand new in the story, and they're already upset. They were upset "…that someone had come to seek the well-being of the Israelites." (Nehemiah 2:10) Nehemiah's whole trip is about helping people, and somebody still wasn't happy about it.
